title: A Taylor and series approximation fan: how good is the approximation, and where?
summary: A function drawn with polynomial approximations of increasing order, and a second panel with the error on a log axis. Inside the radius of convergence the error collapses as the order grows; outside it blows up.

media.alt: Left: a thick white curve 1/(1+x^2) with four coloured polynomial curves of order 2, 4, 8 and 16 that hug it between x = -1 and 1 and fly off outside, on a teal band marked radius R = 1. Right: log-scale error curves collapsing toward x = 0 and rising steeply beyond the dashed orange lines at x = plus or minus 1.
media.caption: Reference render of class F3.7 (design-system gallery). The data are synthetic and exist only to demonstrate the form.

source.note: Plot class from the design system's plot taxonomy; synthetic demonstration data. Standard theory only.

read_the_figure.question: How good is the approximation and where?
read_the_figure.axes: Left: x from -1.6 to 1.6, y from -0.5 to 2.2. Right: x the same, error |f - T_n| on a log axis from 1e-12 to 1e4. Dashed orange lines at x = plus and minus 1 and the teal band mark the radius of convergence. Line style and colour give the order: 2 (dashed blue), 4 (dash-dot amber), 8 (dotted rose), 16 (solid teal).
look_at: Inside the band, what happens to the error as the order increases?
Outside the band, what happens as the order increases?
What is the error exactly at x = plus or minus 1 for every order?
Why does a smooth function like 1/(1 + x^2) have a limited radius?
as_drawn: f(x) = 1/(1 + x^2), Taylor polynomials about 0 of order 2, 4, 8, 16. The radius of convergence is 1 (shaded and dashed).
At x = plus or minus 1 all four error curves cross at 0.5: no improvement at the boundary. At x = 1.6 the order-16 error is 1.3e3 against 1.8 for order 2.
The left panel clips y at 2.2, so the divergence outside the band is cut off, which understates it.
read_the_figure.proves: That the approximation improves with order inside |x| < 1 and degrades outside. It does not by itself say why the radius is 1; that needs the complex plane.
if_wrong: No validity radius marked: a reader will trust the high order everywhere.
Linear error axis: the exponential collapse inside and blow-up outside both disappear.
Only one order shown: no way to see convergence.

terms.meaning: The polynomial of given order built from the derivatives of f at a centre point; it matches f and its first n derivatives there.
The distance from the centre within which the Taylor series converges to f.
The highest power in the polynomial.
The difference between f and its Taylor polynomial.
A series whose ratio between terms is constant, summing to 1/(1 - q) when |q| < 1.
A point where the function is not defined or not analytic; the nearest one, even off the real axis, sets R.

remember: Taylor polynomial: T_n(x) = sum of f^(k)(a)(x - a)^k / k!.
Inside R: error falls as the order rises. Outside R: it grows.
R = distance to the nearest singularity in the complex plane.
Mark R on the plot and label each order.

understand.title: Marks and encodings
understand.text: A thick white line is the exact function; thinner lines in distinct colours and dash patterns are polynomials of orders 2, 4, 8, 16. A shaded band and dashed vertical lines mark the radius. The right panel encodes the error by height on a log axis, so a factor of ten is a fixed distance.

understand.title: Why this form answers the question
understand.text: A polynomial of higher order should be a better fit, and the left panel shows that it is, but only near the centre and only inside the radius. The right panel makes that quantitative: inside the band the curves fall by many decades at small x; outside they rise. The boundary at x = 1 is where all orders meet at the same error, a sign of non-convergence there.

understand.title: How it misleads
understand.text: Plotting only the interval of good behaviour hides the divergence. Clipping the y axis in the left panel hides how large the error gets. A smooth function on the real line can still have a small radius, because the singularities are at plus and minus i: nothing visible on the real axis warns you. And error on a linear scale hides the collapse.

understand.title: Why each required item matters
understand.text: The order labels make the fan readable. The marked radius turns a vague 'works near zero' into a precise statement. Together they give the reader the question to ask: is my x inside R?

understand.title: Alternatives
understand.text: Pade approximants can extend past the radius. Chebyshev interpolants approximate globally on an interval (see Runge's phenomenon). For a convergence picture in the complex plane use the disk plot F3.8. A table of error against order at fixed x is more exact for one point.

understand.title: A variant to create
understand.text: Add an x-order heat map of log error with the contour at 1e-6 and the radius lines; add Pade [4/4] to show it passing the boundary.

steps.title: The Taylor polynomials and their exact error
steps.note: A geometric series with ratio -x^2, summed in closed form. The error magnitude is |x|^(n+2)/(1 + x^2).

steps.title: Convergence only for |x| < 1
steps.note: At x = 0.5: 0.05 for n = 2, 7.8e-4 for n = 8, 3e-6 for n = 16. At x = 1.6: 1.84, 30.9 and 1327. Every order has error 1/2 at x = 1. The radius is the distance from 0 to the poles at plus or minus i.

worked.title: Reading the reference render
worked.problem: From the figure: (1) at x = 0.5 how does the error fall from order 2 to order 8? (2) What happens at x = 1.6? (3) What is the error at x = 1?

solution.text: From about 0.05 (order 2) to 8e-4 (order 8) read on the log scale: about a factor 60.
The error grows with order: order 2 gives 1.8, order 16 gives 1300.

worked.answer: Error falls by a factor 60 from order 2 to 8 at x = 0.5; grows without bound outside the band; equals 1/2 at the boundary for every order.

analyze.q: Why does the order-16 curve beat the others inside the band yet lose outside?
The function is smooth for every real x. Where is the obstacle to a larger radius?
What would you plot to choose the order needed for an error of 1e-6 at x = 0.8?

evaluate.q: An engineer uses a 10th-order Taylor polynomial of a model 'because it fits well on the test data'. When is this safe?
evaluate.hint: Is the test range inside the radius?

checks.q: What is the radius of convergence of the Taylor series of 1/(1 + x^2) about 0?
checks.answer: 1: the poles at plus and minus i are one unit from the origin.

checks.q: At x = 0.5, what is the error of the order-4 polynomial?
The error at x = 1 is the same for every order. What does it tell you?
checks.answer: The series does not converge there: terms do not tend to zero, so adding terms (raising order) does not help.
